title: I knew it not
hook: Jacob wakes: surely the Lord is in this place, and I knew it not (Genesis 28:16)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was holy, the seraphim's word, called three times. Your line was taken apart, then put back together.

A man on the run, alone, with the brother he cheated behind him. That's Jacob in Genesis, long before the day Esau runs to meet him. The sun goes down on him in the middle of nowhere. The King James text is almost offhand: "he lighted upon a certain place, and tarried there all night, because the sun was set". No shrine, nothing to mark it. He takes a stone for a pillow and lies down on the ground. A certain place. Any place.
screen: `JACOB ON THE RUN.` → `A CERTAIN PLACE.` → `A STONE FOR A PILLOW.`

segments.voice: First, the dream: "and behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven: and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it." Notice where the ladder stands: on the earth, right where a tired man is sleeping on a rock. In the dream, heaven isn't somewhere else; it touches down here. Second, the waking: "And Jacob awaked out of his sleep, and he said, Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not." The place didn't change overnight. Jacob did. In his own words, the LORD was in this place when he arrived, when he chose the stone, while he slept. He just didn't know. Third, the fear: "And he was afraid, and said, How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven." Dreadful sounds strange to a modern ear. Here it sits close to awe, the trembling side from the start of this block. Fourth, the new name. Jacob sets up his stone as a pillar and calls the place Bethel. Genesis adds that the city had been called Luz before. The same ground, two names: one from before he knew, one from after. For Jews and Christians, Bethel is a place where God met Jacob. For anyone, it raises a quiet question: how many certain places, ordinary as a roadside, do people pass through without knowing?
screen: `A LADDER SET UP ON THE EARTH.` · `THE PLACE DIDN'T CHANGE. JACOB DID.` · `HOW DREADFUL IS THIS PLACE.` · `LUZ BECOMES BETHEL.` · then, large: `AND I KNEW IT NOT.`

segments.voice: Stay exactly where you are, and look at this place as if you'd just woken up in it after a long journey: the corners, the light, the sounds, what you've stopped seeing because it's always here. Then, if it feels right, say Jacob's words quietly: and I knew it not. If you pray, you can say the whole line; if not, the looking is enough.
Bethel. The place Jacob named on waking, where in his telling the LORD had been there all along, and he was the one who changed. Today's word.
Your line: and I knew it not. Luz before, Bethel after: the same ground, two names. Day one thousand five.

howItsDone: Jews and Christians read Jacob's dream at Bethel in Genesis 28 as a story of God meeting a person in an unexpected place; some people repeat Jacob's words when they notice an ordinary place anew.

chat.meaning: Waking from the ladder dream, Jacob said, Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not. The place didn't change overnight; Jacob did.

notes: Hook calls Jacob 'a young man' and says 'long before the day Esau runs to meet him' (Genesis 33): Genesis 31:41 has Jacob serving twenty years, but his age at Bethel isn't stated. Trim 'young' if the auditor prefers.
'Dreadful ... sits close to awe' reads the KJV word by context; check.
The original-game note links Bethel to 'house of God' in verse 17, which the text itself sets side by side; a Hebraist should confirm spelling.
For a Jewish reader, JPS 1917 may be preferred for Genesis 28.

Audit: the narrator stated as fact that the place 'had been holy' all along and that heaven 'touches down here'; both now attributed to the dream and to Jacob's own words. Jewish readers differ on whether the place was holy before (Rashi links it to Moriah) or became so in the vision; a Keeper may add this.
Editor: 'no town worth naming' changed, since 28:19 names the city Luz; the earlier note about 'a young man' is stale (the hook already says 'a man').
